title: Ad or Info?
tagline: Students sort mock posts, videos, and headlines into ads, information, and clickbait, hunt for persuasion tricks, and then create an honest, clearly labeled ad of their own.
groupSize: Teams of 3–4 for the sort; pairs for the ad; any class size
overview: Kids see ads everywhere, and many don't look like ads: a favorite gamer's "honest review," a sponsored search result, a cartoon inside a free game, a shocking headline built to get a click. In this lesson teams sort fourteen mock media items into **Ad** (wants you to buy), **Info** (wants you to know), and **Clickbait** (wants you to click), using a Persuasion Detective checklist. Then pairs flip roles and become media makers, creating an honest ad for a made-up product, labeled so no one is fooled. Along the way they see that AI can write persuasive text in seconds, which makes spotting persuasion a skill everyone needs.
objectives: Students will classify media items as ads, information, or clickbait and cite the clue that shows the creator's purpose.
Students will name at least three persuasion techniques (hurry words, bandwagon, famous endorser, too-good-to-be-true, mystery headline) and find them in examples.
Students will create an honest, clearly labeled ad and explain how it differs from an information piece about the same product.
Students will explain that AI tools can produce persuasive text quickly, so readers need to ask who made something and why.

print: Handout A: Ad, Info, or Clickbait? sort strips (1 set per team, cut apart, with the sorting mat)
Handout B: Persuasion Detective checklist (1 per team)
Handout C: Make an Honest Ad (1 per pair)
Colored pencils or markers; three corner signs: AD, INFO, CLICKBAIT
digital: Optional: a generative AI chatbot your district approves, on the teacher's device, projected for the class
Optional: screenshots you capture in advance of a kid-safe search results page that includes items labeled "Sponsored"
Optional: a slide or drawing tool students already use, for making the honest ad digitally

prep: Print and cut Handout A so each team has 14 strips and one sorting mat.
Post AD, INFO, and CLICKBAIT signs in three corners for the whole-class check.
Read the key (the "why" lines) and mark the three trickiest strips (the gamer's promo code, the homework app, and the sponsored search result) for discussion.
If you'll run the AI demo, test the prompt from the Digital section in your district-approved chatbot first.

steps.title: The cereal review
steps.body: Read aloud, with a big smile: **"Hey friends! I just tried CloudCrunch cereal and it's honestly the best breakfast ever. It gives you SO much energy. Everybody at my school is eating it!"** Ask: "Would you try CloudCrunch?" Then reveal the tiny line at the bottom: **#ad · Paid partnership with CloudCrunch.** Ask: "Does that change what you think? Why?"
steps.note: CloudCrunch is a made-up brand. Many students will say the review now feels less trustworthy. Ask why being paid might change what someone says.

steps.title: Three questions and the detective checklist
steps.body: Write three questions on the board: **Who made this? What do they want me to do: buy, know, or click? What clues tell me?** Walk through Handout B, the Persuasion Detective checklist, giving a quick example of each technique. Then model one strip from Handout A: "'You WON'T BELIEVE what this cat did next!!!' Who made it? I don't know. What do they want? A click. Clues: ALL CAPS, three exclamation points, a mystery with no answer. Clickbait."
steps.note: Clarify that ads aren't bad. People make and sell things. The problem is when you can't tell something is an ad.

steps.title: Team sort
steps.body: Teams sort the 14 strips onto their mat, using Handout B to check clues. The team must agree on each strip, and anyone can say "Prove it" to ask for the clue. After 8 minutes, run a fast corner check: read five strips aloud and have one member of each team walk to the corner their team chose and name the clue.
steps.note: Strips 12 and 13 are designed to split the room: they are ads that don't say "ad." Push teams to find the clue (a promo code, a product pitch inside an answer).

steps.title: The sneaky ones
steps.body: Ask: **"Which strips were hardest? What made them sneaky?"** Focus on the gamer's promo code (a clue he may be paid, even without #ad), the homework app's answer that ends with a product pitch, and the sponsored search result that sits at the top. Ask: "How is an ad hiding inside a helpful answer different from a label that says 'Sponsored'?" Then ask: "If a computer can write a persuasive ad in five seconds, what does that mean for us as readers?"
steps.note: If you do the AI demo, run it here. Students hunt for persuasion techniques in the AI-written ad using Handout B.

steps.title: Make an honest ad
steps.body: Pairs complete Handout C for a made-up product (Pencil Pal, the eraser that never smudges; or a product they invent). They design an honest ad that uses at most two persuasion techniques, includes a clear "AD" label, and makes no promises that aren't true. Then they write a short **info** version about the same product: just the facts. Pairs swap with another pair, who checks it using Handout B and says which techniques they spotted.
steps.note: This is S5.2 creativity with limits: students must persuade honestly. Look for labels and facts they could actually back up.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: On the back of Handout C, students finish: "The next time I see a video or post about a product, I will ask ___." and "The persuasion trick I'll watch out for most is ___ because ___."
steps.note: Strong answers name a specific question ("Is this person being paid?") rather than "is it real?"

unplugged: The sort, checklist, and ad creation all run on paper. The corner check adds movement. For the AI part without a screen, read aloud the idea that computers can now write ads in seconds and have students write a 30-second ad themselves, timing it, to feel how fast persuasive text can be produced.
digital: During the Debrief, project a district-approved AI chatbot and type as the class watches: "Write a short, exciting ad for kids for a made-up eraser called Pencil Pal." Students use Handout B to find the persuasion techniques in the result and check whether it made any promises that couldn't be true. You can also show screenshots, captured in advance, of a kid-safe search results page with items labeled "Sponsored." Students can build their honest ad in a slide or drawing tool the class already uses. Students under 13 never use their own AI accounts; the teacher drives the chatbot.
whyTech: The sort works fully on paper. The projected AI demo adds evidence paper can't: students watch a tool produce a slick, persuasive ad in seconds and then pick it apart with the checklist, which shows why spotting persuasion matters more, not less, with AI in the world.

adaptations.label: Grade 3
adaptations.text: Use two categories (Ad and Info) with 10 strips, then introduce Clickbait as a bonus round with strips 3, 7, and 10.

adaptations.label: Grade 5
adaptations.text: Add a fourth category, "Both," for items that mix info and selling, and have teams defend one item they placed there.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: Pre-teach "ad," "sponsored," "persuade," and "clickbait" with visuals; let students create their honest ad in either language.

adaptations.label: Students who need fewer strips
adaptations.text: Give a team 7 strips (one from each clear category plus the tricky ones) and a partner who reads aloud.

lookFors: Teams cite a specific clue (#ad, Sponsored label, promo code, hurry words, a pitch inside an answer) for each tricky strip.
Students find persuasion techniques in the AI-written ad and flag any claim that couldn't be true.
Honest ads on Handout C include a clear AD label and no false promises; the info version sticks to facts.
Exit tickets name a specific question to ask about product posts.
reflection: Am I good at using different tools to help me learn? How do I know when a post is trying to sell me something? (Student ELE guiding question)
Which persuasion trick works best on you? Why?
How did it feel to try to persuade someone honestly?
transfer: Students go on an "ad hunt" at home with a family member, finding one ad that says it's an ad and one that doesn't, and noting the clue for each on the back of Handout C. Next lesson, *Credit Where It's Due* builds on being an honest media maker.

handouts.title: Ad, Info, or Clickbait?
handouts.instructions: All brands and people here are made up. Sort each strip. Be ready to say the clue that proves it.

items.text: A kid unboxes ZoomBlaster sneakers on video: "These make you run faster!" Small text: #ad Paid partnership with ZoomBlaster.
items.why: The #ad label shows he is paid. "Run faster" is a too-good-to-be-true promise.

items.text: A library web page: "How to Care for a Pet Hamster," written by a veterinarian, with no products for sale.
items.why: An expert explains; nothing is being sold.

items.text: "You WON'T BELIEVE what this cat did next!!! Click NOW!"
items.why: Mystery headline, ALL CAPS, and exclamation points to get a click.

items.text: In a free game: "Get 500 gems now! Only $4.99! Offer ends in 10 minutes!"
items.why: Hurry words and a price. The timer pushes you to buy fast.

items.text: A kids' news article: "Pinewood Opens New Public Pool This Summer," with the date and the reporter's name.
items.why: It names who wrote it and when, and reports news.

items.text: The weather page says: "Tomorrow: sunny, high of 85°F."
items.why: Just facts you need; nothing to buy or click.

items.text: "Kids HATE this one weird trick to never do homework again!"
items.why: A "weird trick" and a promise that sounds too good to be true.

items.text: A cartoon character in a free app says: "Ask your parents to buy Sparkle Slime Deluxe today!"
items.why: A favorite character is used to sell a product to kids.

items.text: A museum website explains how volcanoes erupt, with a labeled diagram.
items.why: It teaches; nothing is for sale.

items.text: "Top 10 Scariest Animals: Number 7 Will SHOCK You!" with a blurry photo.
items.why: Built to make you click through a list to find out.

items.text: The school newsletter: "Picture day is Thursday. Wear your best smile!"
items.why: The school is sharing a date you need.

items.text: A popular gamer posts: "I only play with the TurboPad controller! Use my code TURBO10 for a discount." There is no #ad label.
items.why: A personal discount code is a clue he may earn money from sales, even without a label.

items.text: A homework helper app answers a question about plants, then ends: "For even better grades, upgrade to BrightPath Premium today!"
items.why: A sales pitch is hiding at the end of a helpful answer.

items.text: The top search result has a small "Sponsored" label: "SnackStar Chips: The Crunch Everyone Loves!"
items.why: "Sponsored" means the company paid to be at the top. "Everyone loves" is bandwagon.

handouts.title: Persuasion Detective
handouts.instructions: Use this checklist on any strip, video, or AI-written ad. Mark each clue Found it or Not here.
items: Someone is paid: #ad, Sponsored, Partner, or a special promo code
Hurry words: now, today only, ends soon, a countdown timer
A famous or favorite person or character is selling it
Too good to be true: run faster, never do homework, best ever
ALL CAPS and lots of !!! to grab attention
Mystery headline: "You won't believe…," "Number 7 will shock you"
A sales pitch hiding inside something helpful
I can tell who made it and what they want me to do

handouts.title: Make an Honest Ad
handouts.instructions: Pick a made-up product (Pencil Pal, the eraser that never smudges, or invent your own). Persuade honestly!

sections.prompt: Our product and what it really does:
Draw our honest ad. Include a clear AD label.
The persuasion techniques we used (no more than 2) and why they're honest:
Now write an INFO version about the same product. Just the facts:
What is the biggest difference between our ad and our info version?
Partner check: Which techniques did the other pair spot in our ad?
